description: After OAuth authentication started from My Places GPX upload, the authorization-completion callback dismisses the login sheet without forwarding completion to its target fragment. Investigate the missing continuation of the upload workflow.

Sharing an exported file using a file URI raises FileUriExposedException on newer Android versions. The task concerns cross-application file-URI exposure and compatible sharing, not arbitrary exported components.
The Android application has not explicitly opted out of WebView usage-statistics collection. Investigate the privacy configuration concern described in the public change record.

On Android API 30, source-folder operations request a Storage Access Framework dialog even though the application already has read permission. Investigate the source-path permission and storage-flow mismatch.
An encrypted MMS with malformed Base64 encoding can lead to a null-pointer exception during message decoding. Investigate validation and null handling of the decoded input.

The custom OAuth authorization URL is constructed by concatenating a configurable host and authorization path directly. Investigate path-boundary handling when the two parts provide inconsistent slashes.
The app-common Android manifest is outside the source-set location used by the Android module. Investigate whether the intended manifest declarations participate in the build.

A Fragment-lifetime coroutine consumes JavaScript requests and dereferences a WebView binding that is set to null in onDestroyView. Requests arriving after view destruction can access an invalid view binding.

When enabling an open proxy on all interfaces on Android API 37+, local-network permission may be absent or revoked outside the application. Investigate permission requests and reconciliation of the saved preference with the granted state.

When a room participant logs out, removed devices are deleted from the Realm device collection while that collection is being iterated. Investigate collection invalidation and the resulting encrypted-message failure.
Sensitive contact-list screens are not consistently protected against screen capture. Investigate coverage of the secure-window flag across passphrase-protected screens.
Text-to-speech service discovery fails when targeting Android 11 because the manifest does not declare the required package-visibility query for TTS services.

For message-body push conditions, wordsOnly is enabled only for RULE_ID_CONTAIN_USER_NAME. Other body patterns use simpleGlobToRegExp().containsMatchIn(value), so a body pattern can match a substring instead of the required whole-word boundary. Investigate this body-rule semantic regression.

Every map-index load reconstructs a set of standard POI key names by walking categories and types, even though the standard set is invariant for that process. Investigate redundant repeated computation.
Link parsing visits individual Text nodes but repeatedly scans the full rendered text for links. A long message containing many paragraphs causes repeated full-text work and poor parsing performance.
Browser-card rendering emits notifyDataSetChanged for every card in a large initial batch. The repeated UI refreshes delay the long-click listener and make the browser unresponsive during rendering.

Audio-stream selection loops while no result is found. With an empty stream list and a non-null preferred format, the loop neither finds an item nor reaches its break condition, causing an ANR when called on the UI thread.

When starting Tor in power-user mode, setup can return before permission is granted while the connect switch remains checked. Investigate consistency between the user-visible switch and the unfinished connection setup; battery-optimization prompts are related context.

The passphrase dialog onCreate path checks only the original PASSPHRASE type. Other text-entry authentication types may not display the required fragment after the unconditional display path was removed.

Helper.isSecure uses Settings.System.LOCK_PATTERN_ENABLED only on API levels below 23 and KeyguardManager.isDeviceSecure on API 23 and above. The public change concerns prospective migration away from a deprecated lock-screen setting; no present unguarded new-API call or reproduced crash is asserted.
The beta build variant does not register the feature-flag override dependency required by initialization. Investigate the missing dependency-injection binding during startup of that variant.

APKG export uses different directories across compatibility implementations: the collection-parent export directory in CompatV10 and the app files directory in CompatV16. AnkiPackageExporter also deletes intermediate SQLite files with File.delete without database-sidecar cleanup. Treat export-directory consistency and database cleanup as separate facets of this export workflow.

Root-mode startup writes an exec command to the su process but returns before flushing the command stream. The buffered startup command may never reach the process, leaving the application waiting for the binary to start.
The built-in Runbox IMAP provider hostname is incorrect, so automatic account configuration points to the wrong mail server.

Apps that use the *call()* in the Content Provider API are vulnerable to exposing the underlying data store to unauthorized read and write. The Content provider API provides a method *call(String method, String args, Bundle extras)* to call any provider-defined method. Android does no permission checking on this entry into the content provider besides the basic ability for the application to get access to the provider at all. For example, Android has no idea whether *call* will read or write data in the provider, so can't enforce those individual permissions.
Any implementation of this method must do its own permission checks on incoming calls to make sure they are allowed. Failure to do so will allow unauthorized components to interact with the content provider.

Apps that do not handle *unchecked exceptions* are vulnerable to *Denial of Service* attack. If an app has code which might throw exceptions under some circumstances, then an app developer is responsible to handle them explicitly. *Malicious* app may try to execute the part of the app which throws the exception but is not handled by an app developer by passing some arbitrary arguments if needed.

MyReceiver is explicitly exported in the Benign AndroidManifest.xml without a component permission and performs privileged operations. Investigate access by an untrusted broadcasting application to this unprotected receiver.

Apps are vulnerable to phishing attacks and denial of serivce attacks if the device contains malicious apps that use Task-reparenting. An activity M in a malicious app can use task affinity and task re-parenting to request to start/launch M in the same task as that of an activity in a benign app and as the top of that task, thereby allowing activity M to launch a Denial-Of-Service attack or a Phishing attack.

MyIntentService uses SSLCertificateSocketFactory.createSocket(InetAddress, port). Investigate missing hostname validation for this overload. Certificate-chain trust and empty checkServerTrusted implementations are separate concerns, not the declared hostname target.

Apps that do not pin the certificates of servers they trust are
vulnerable to MITM attacks. Apps can be vulnerable if they do not implement a certificate pinning. If a certificate authority mistakenly trusts the Malicious server, then the app which does not implement the pinning, will end up trusting the Malicious server.
Apps that communicate with a remote server over an open port are vulnerable to information leak.

MyIntentService configures HttpsURLConnection with SSLCertificateSocketFactory.getInsecure and a HostnameVerifier whose verify method always returns true. Investigate these two explicit bypasses of TLS peer verification.

Apps using outdated libraries containing vulnerabilities may themselves be vulnerable. When an app uses an external library, it may use older versions of the library which may contain vulnerabilities. As a result, the app may exhibit vulnerabilities.
Apps that use more permissions than they need are vulnerable to privilege escalation attacks.

Apps that use *SQLiteDatabase.execSQL()* method to construct non-parameterized SQL queries are vulnerable to SQL injection attacks. If an app uses inputs (e.g., user input via UI or data from web) to create a SQL statement to be executed via *execSQL()* method, then the app may be vulnerable to *SQL-injection attack*.
Apps that write sensitive information to files stored in External Storage can potentially leak sensitive information.

DownloadService is explicitly exported without a component permission in the Benign AndroidManifest.xml. An external application can invoke the download workflow that copies internal data to external storage. Investigate this unprotected exported service entry and the associated data transfer.

Apps that use *SQLiteDatabase.rawQuery()* method to construct non-parameterized SQL queries are vulnerable to SQL injection attacks. If the app does not parameterize the queries it uses to interact with the database then it is vulnerable to SQL injection attacks.

Apps that use *checkCallingOrSelfPermission* to verify access control are vulnerable
to privilege escalation attacks. A component that uses run-time permission checking via *checkCallingOrSelfPermission* for access control, grants permission to **all** components if it grants permission even once to a component that is in the same app as that of itself. 
If *checkCallingOrSelfPermission* is used to protect a component that performs a sensitive operation then a component in a malicious app 
can escalate its privilege and access the component.

Apps that use *enforceCallingOrSelfPermission* to verify access control are vulnerable
to privilege escalation attacks. A component that uses run-time permission checking via *enforceCallingOrSelfPermission* for access control, grants permission to **all** components if it grants permission even once to a component that is in the same app as that of itself. 
If *enforceCallingOrSelfPermission* is used to protect a component that performs a sensitive operation then a component in a malicious app 
can escalate its privilege and access the component.

Apps that allow copying of *sensitive information to clipboard* may leak information. Since every app has access to the content of the clipboard independent of the
source (app) of the content, malicious apps can �steal� information by merely accessing
the clipboard.

Apps that use device identifiers to uniquely identify app instances are vulnerable to exposing device-specific sensitive information. Collecting device identifiers could lead to exposing sensitive data related to the 
device which can be used by malicious actors to track the device.

Apps that allow websites viewed through WebView may enable *cookie overwrite* attacks. An Android that uses WebView can allow websites to store cookies. A malicious web page *MW* from the same domain as benign web page *BW* can overwrite cookies set by *BW* by specifying the same name/domain/path.

The Benign WebView enables JavaScript, setAllowFileAccess(true), and setAllowFileAccessFromFileURLs(true). Investigate untrusted script access to local resources through this same WebView; JavaScript-interface bridging is not the specified mechanism.

Apps that allow Javascript code execution in WebView widget may be susceptible to malicious code execution. If arbitrary web content is loaded into WebView without disabling JavaScript code execution,
an adversary could inject malicious code through JavaScript and have it executed by an app to cause harm.

Apps that connect to a server via the *HTTP* protocol are vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks. A MITM can easily intercept traffic between the app and the server and can even spoof the address of the server to masquerade as the server to the app.

The Benign WebView loads HTML using a file-scheme baseURL in loadDataWithBaseURL and enables JavaScript, file access, and setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true). Investigate this combined local-origin and cross-origin resource exposure.

The Benign WebView enables setAllowContentAccess(true), JavaScript, and setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs(true). Investigate whether untrusted script in this WebView can reach content-provider resources available to the application.
The expected state sequence is Start -> Active -> Pause -> Restore -> Active -> Destroy. Violating this sequence may cause Activity errors.
android:configChanges is not declared in AndroidManifest.xml, causing the system to recreate the Activity by default.
Insufficient understanding of the Android task stack and launchMode causes navigation behavior to violate user expectations.
A Fragment depends on its host Activity and cannot run independently. Its lifecycle is closely coupled to the host Activity lifecycle.
If event handlers for some states are missing, the application may enter an incorrect state or crash.
Developers must correctly implement the callbacks invoked by Android when configuration settings change.
The design or implementation of control flow, such as conditional branches, loops, or state machines, is incorrect.
Object lifecycle management or object usage violates programming conventions; this is a basic coding-practice defect.
Parsing, conversion, or validation of data formats is handled incorrectly.
Conditional branches such as if or switch are missing or contain logic errors.
A function or method call omits required arguments, or argument validation is incomplete.
An arithmetic result may exceed the range representable by its destination variable type, violating the numeric-range contract and potentially producing an incorrect value.
User input, network input, or interprocess communication data is not properly validated.
Object initialization is incomplete or violates its design specification.
A variable or object has an incorrect initial value, or required initialization logic is missing.
The same property uses different default values in different scenarios or modules, making behavior unpredictable.
The same property is used inconsistently across contexts, with conflicting types, ranges, or meanings, violating programming consistency.
A Preference XML resource uses invalid nesting, such as an int directly inside PreferenceScreen instead of a Preference child, violating the preference hierarchy expected by the platform parser.
Android framework mechanisms, such as lifecycle management or event callbacks, are handled incorrectly.
An Android application resource is defined or used incorrectly, such as a layout, icon, or resource ID of a UI element.
An Android framework API is used incorrectly, either violating its constraints or choosing an inappropriate API.
An Activity is used where ApplicationContext should be used.
The Android framework has a design defect, undocumented limitation, or implementation vulnerability that ordinary application programming conventions cannot avoid.
Versions, interfaces, or compatibility of a third-party library are managed incorrectly.
A third-party library has an unfixed vulnerability, implementation error, or functional limitation.
A service or library has an inherent defect, obsolete or deprecated version, or hidden dependency conflict.

Sensitive information is stored by SharedPreferences in its default plaintext XML format without encryption, violating confidentiality at rest. A subject able to read the file can obtain the plaintext information.
There is a risk of SQL injection or plaintext storage of sensitive data.
There is plaintext-storage risk, inappropriate file permissions, or missing data validation.
A file:// URL directly accesses an application private directory, such as /data/data/pkg_name/, bypassing Android sandbox restrictions.
An untrusted input stream is deserialized without validating its origin and type. Attacker-controlled serialized input may instantiate unintended classes.

On historical Android versions that support it, the application creates a file using deprecated MODE_WORLD_WRITABLE. Other applications can modify its contents, enabling data tampering or malicious code injection.
The issue may invalidate encryption and may even be more dangerous than using no encryption.

MD5 hashing is used in a security-sensitive context requiring collision resistance, such as integrity verification or authentication. The collision-resistance contract is violated and the verification mechanism may fail.
SHA-1 hashing is used in a security-sensitive context requiring collision resistance, such as integrity verification, digital signatures, or authentication. The verification mechanism may fail.
Base64 encoding is mistakenly used as confidentiality protection for sensitive data, rather than as ordinary encoding. A reader can reverse the encoding without a key.
DES with only a 56-bit key encrypts sensitive data, violating the requirement for sufficient symmetric-key strength. The plaintext can be recovered by feasible brute force.
A PendingIntent is created without a valid base Intent, violating the requirement to encapsulate a defined target operation. A recipient cannot resolve and handle the intended operation.

A Service declares android:exported=true in AndroidManifest.xml, expanding cross-application access. Without permission or code-level access restrictions, external applications can bind to or start it.

A ContentProvider declares android:exported=true in AndroidManifest.xml, expanding cross-application access. Without permission or code-level restrictions, external applications can query or modify its data.
